region.text: Zhu Yuanzhang's Wu: Yingtian (Nanjing), the lower Yangtze, Anhui, Zhejiang, Jiangxi and Huguang, renamed the Ming

ledger.note: 1368: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims the Ming at Nanjing (Yingtian). 'On 23 January 1368, Zhu proclaimed himself emperor and renamed his state.' The page gives the proclamation, not a boundary: the core is the Wu's lower Yangtze, Anhui, Jiangxi and Huguang (see the zhu-yuanzhang-s-wu dossier).
1368: the Ming take Fujian. 'They had easily conquered Fujian by February 1368.'
1368: the Ming take Shandong. 'By March 1368, Ming land and naval forces had captured Shandong.'
1368: the Ming take Guangdong. 'taken control of Guangdong by April.'
1368: the Ming occupy Henan. 'Henan was occupied in May.'
1368: Guangxi comes under the Ming. 'Guangxi was brought under Ming control by July 1368.'

1368: the Ming reach Dadu and the Yuan court flees to the steppe. 'The Ming army resumed its march in mid-August and reached Dadu (present-day Beijing) in early September'; the Ming page adds 'the city was renamed Beiping in the same year'. The page gives no day.
1369: Hebei, bridging. The page names only Dadu (September 1368); Cliopatria's 1375 shape holds all of Hebei and no page opened dates its conquest, so the province is dated here by inference.
1369: Taiyuan falls and Shanxi is the Ming's. The page has Taiyuan captured in January 1369, forcing Köke Temür 'to retreat to Gansu'. The page names the city; the province is the reading.
1369: Shaanxi is the Ming's. 'Ming troops also began operations in Shaanxi in the spring of 1369. They had fully captured the province by September 1369.'

region.text: the Inner Mongolian steppe south of the Gobi, where the Ming and the Yuan remnant fought

ledger.note: 1370: the Ming attack Mongolia. 'In 1370, the Ming government launched a two-pronged attack on Mongolia'; 'Köke Temür was defeated in early May and fled to Karakorum.' The Yuan court, driven north in 1368, becomes the Northern Yuan (northern-yuan dossier, which also opens the zone in 1370).

region.text: Yingchang and the steppe margin that Cliopatria's 1375 shape gives the Ming

ledger.note: 1370: Yingchang taken. 'In June, Li conquered Yingchang.' The page gives no modern location, so the Ming's share of the Inner Mongolian steppe is read from Cliopatria's 1375 shape.

region.text: Tibetan areas: Prince Punala's tribute, then the 1372-73 envoys to renew Yuan titles in Kham and the south-east

ledger.note: 1371: Tibet pays tribute to the Ming. Prince Punala 'went to Nanjing in 1371 to pay tribute and show his allegiance to the Ming court'; the page's lead calls the relation 'suzerainty' (non-PRC scholars) and the PRC claims 'full sovereignty', while Goldstein holds 'the Ming had no real administrative authority over Tibet'. Drawn as the lightest tint; contested.

1371: Sichuan falls to the Ming. 'By September 1371, Sichuan had been conquered.' (The ming-xia dossier has Chongqing in August and Chengdu in September.) Region narrowed in the fx-09 review to Sichuan without Kham, the Ming Xia land the ming-xia dossier draws; the gain only ever moved Ming Xia's cells.

1372: Okinawa begins tribute to the Ming. 'The first Ming dynasty envoy visits Okinawa'; the tributary relationship was 'begun by Chūzan in 1372'. The island unites only in 1429 (Cliopatria's Ryukyu row starts then; the ryukyu-kingdom dossier has the tribute from 1429).

1372: Feng Sheng takes the Gansu Corridor. 'In the west, Feng Sheng was assigned to conquer the western part of the Gansu Corridor with 50,000 cavalrymen'; the page says Feng's forces completed their mission although the Mongols defeated Xu Da's and Li Wenzhong's armies in the north. The page names the corridor, not the province; the region is the whole of Gansu, as Cliopatria's 1375 and 1385 shapes hold it. Moved here from the confidence-1 line of 1374 (fx-09).

region.text: Ningxia, Guizhou and Hainan: page silent

ledger.note: 1374: Ningxia, Guizhou and Hainan, bridging. Cliopatria's 1375 Ming shape holds them and its Yuan row ends in 1374, but the Hongwu page dates none of them (it does not mention Ningxia, Guizhou or Hainan). Gansu is dated 1372 by the line above (fx-09).

region.text: the remaining Yuan-held territory in Yunnan

ledger.note: 1381: the Ming invade Yunnan. 'Some 250,000 to 300,000 Han and Hui Muslim troops were mobilized to crush the remaining Yuan-held territory in Yunnan in 1381.' The counterpart is the Yuan prince of Liang, Basalawarmi, whose Yunnan has no Cliopatria shape; northern-yuan is the nearest dossier.
1382: the Yuan prince of Liang is dead and Yunnan falls. Basalawarmi 'committed suicide on January 6, 1382.'

1382: Yunnan is the Ming's. 'In 1382 Lan Yu and Mu Ying's forces attacked and crushed Duan's realm after a fierce battle.' The Ming page puts it as 'In 1381, the Ming dynasty annexed the areas of the southwest that had once been part of the Kingdom of Dali.'
1383: the last Dali stronghold falls. 'The last Dali stronghold of Dengchuan fell to the Ming in February 1383'; the Duan family were taken to Nanjing.

region.text: Luchuan, the Möng Mao tusi (modern Ruili and northern Myanmar)

ledger.note: 1386: Möng Mao rebels against the Ming. In Luchuan (modern Ruili and northern Myanmar), 'Möng Mao forces rebelled against the Ming from 1386 to 1389.' The shan-states dossier dates the first attack to 1385 from another page.

1387: the Ming march on Naghachu in Manchuria. 'In 1387 the Ming sent a military campaign to attack Naghachu.' Naghachu was the Yuan loyalist commander in Manchuria; northern-yuan is the nearest dossier.

1387: Naghachu surrenders. The campaign 'concluded with the surrender of Naghachu and Ming conquest of Manchuria'; the Hongwu page agrees: 'The campaign into Manchuria in 1387 was ultimately successful.' The region is the southern Manchuria of Cliopatria's 1385 shape; the page names only 'Manchuria'.

region.text: the Inner Mongolian steppe south of the Gobi

ledger.note: 1388: the Mongols are beaten at Buir Lake. Lan Yu's army 'decisively defeated the Mongols at the Songhua River and Buir Lake'; the 1370 zone ends.
1388: the Manchurian campaign ends. The 1387-88 campaign closes at the Songhua River and Buir Lake.
1388: the Ming annex the Liaodong peninsula. 'The campaign also resulted in the annexation of the Liaodong Peninsula.'
1389: the first Möng Mao rebellion ends ('from 1386 to 1389').
1397: Möng Mao rebels again, 'from 1397 to 1398'.
1398: the second Möng Mao rebellion ends.

1401: Joseon enters the Ming tributary system. 'Joseon joined the Imperial Chinese tributary system in 1401'; infobox 'Tributary relations with the Ming and Qing (1401-1895)'. Cliopatria's 'Allegiance of Joseon to Ming' relation runs 1395-1571, which the page does not support.

region.text: the Jianzhou Jurchens east of Fushun and Kaiyuan

ledger.note: 1403: the Jianzhou Guard is set up. 'Ahacu, chief of the Huligai, became commander of the Jianzhou Guard in 1403'; the guards 'engaged in trade with the Ming at the designated market of Kaiyuan and Fushun' and 'Jurchens began accepting Ming titles.' The land is the page's 'modern-day Liaoning and Jilin', read as the country east of Fushun.
1404: Hami accepts Ming supremacy. 'The Ming dynasty established this region as Kumul Hami in 1404 after the Mongol kingdom Qara Del accepted its supremacy.'

region.text: the Red River Delta and its two capitals

ledger.note: 1406: the Ming invade Đại Ngu. 'On 19 November 1406, they captured the two capitals and other important cities in the Red River Delta.'
1407: the Hồ are captured. 'Hồ Quý Ly and his son were captured on 16 June 1407.'

1407: Annam becomes the Ming province of Jiaozhi. 'In July 1407, Yongle changed the name of Annam to Jiaozhi'; 'The province was further divided into fifteen prefectures, 41 subprefectures and 210 counties.'

region.text: the lower Amur at Nurgan (Tyr), 'established in Manchuria (including modern-day Northeast China and Outer Manchuria)'

ledger.note: 1409: the Nurgan Regional Military Commission is founded on the Amur. 'The seat was nominally established in 1409'; the Ming obtained 'at least the nominal allegiance of the lower Amur's tribes'. A vassal tint, not direct rule.

1421: the Ming court moves from Nanjing to Beijing. 'In 1421, the Ming capital was relocated from Nanjing in the south to Beijing in the north'; the Ming page: 'Beijing designated as capital: 28 October 1420', construction 1407-1420.

region.text: the Ming province of Jiaozhi as the rebels take it back

ledger.note: 1424: the Lam Sơn rebels take Nghệ An. They begin 'advancing to liberate Nghệ An' in late 1424 after the uprising of 7 February 1418 at Lam Sơn, and by 1426-27 'The Ming army only controlled two major strongholds', Đông Quan and Thanh Hóa.
1427: the Ming retreat. 'The retreat of the Ming army after the Đông Quan oath' (infobox, 10 December 1427); the Lê dynasty is founded in April 1428.
1427: the Ming give up Vietnam. The Ming general 'was allowed to withdraw his troops safely back to China'; the Ming page: 'until the Ming withdrawal in 1427'.
1435: the Nurgan seat is abandoned. 'The seat was nominally established in 1409, but was abandoned in 1435.'

region.text: Möng Mao (Luchuan-Pingmian): Jinchi, east of the Salween

ledger.note: 1438: the first Ming expedition against Möng Mao. 'The first punitive expedition' reached 'the garrison town of Jinchi, located east of the Salween River' in December 1438; Fang Zheng was defeated at Kongni in January 1439. Four campaigns follow (1441, 1443, 1449).

1449: the last Luchuan-Pingmian campaign ends. 'The fourth and final campaign to extirpate the Mong Mao threat was launched under the supervision of Wang Ji' in March 1449; 'Si Jifa managed to escape yet again, and the campaign ended inconclusively.'

region.text: the Inner Mongolian, Ningxia and Shaanxi margins that Cliopatria's 1450 shape drops

ledger.note: 1450: the steppe margin falls back. Cliopatria removes 2,089 Inner Mongolia cells, Ningxia and Gansu margins from the Ming; the Tumu page says 'There were no territorial changes' after the capture of Zhengtong (1 September 1449 on that page, 8 September on the Ming page), while the Great Wall page says the crisis 'caused the collapse of the early Ming security system'. Bridging; the date is Cliopatria's.

the Hexi Corridor east of Jiayu Pass (Ganzhou and Suzhou), Ming since 1370

region.text: Qinghai and western Gansu: page silent; the Hexi Corridor east of Jiayu Pass stays Ming

ledger.note: 1468: Qinghai and western Gansu leave the Ming map. Cliopatria drops 1,535 Qinghai and 634 Gansu cells in 1468 and no page opened dates or explains it; the Great Wall page has the Ordos wall proposed in August 1471, which shows the Ordos was outside Ming control by then. Bridging; Hami is not part of this loss. [Checked again fx-42, 2 Nov 2026 (dossier request R052): still no page dates a take-over in 1468. Hexi Corridor page: 'In 1370, the newly-established Ming dynasty seized the eastern section of the Hexi Corridor from the Mongols' and 'captured most of the remaining territory in 1372'; Jiayu Pass, built in 1370, 'left the city [Dunhuang] under the control of the Northern Yuan dynasty'; 'In 1524, Jiayu Pass was closed and Dunhuang was occupied by the Turfan Khanate'; the Ming 'rebuilt the Great Wall through the Hexi Corridor from 1539-1541 and added an extension in 1573'. Qinghai page: 'under the control of early Ming dynasty, but later gradually lost to the Khoshut Khanate' (no year), 'From 1640 to 1724' Khoshut control. So the 1468 date is Cliopatria's and stays a bridge (confidence 1); the land west of the pass was not Ming after 1370 (the 1450-1467 shape overdraws it), and about 130 Gansu cells east of the pass (98.3-100.5 E, 39-40 N) that Cliopatria's later shapes lack may be Ming up to the wall years: not corrected here, because the pages give no extent or year for a Ming hold there and every Ming keyframe from 1468 to 1642 would have to carry it.] [orchestrator, 3 Nov 2026, fx-52 handoff: the corridor east of Jiayu Pass is no longer part of this loss]
1513: Hami is lost. 'Hami was conquered and converted to Islam in 1513.' The page does not name the conqueror (Turpan, on other pages); the Ming's supremacy since 1404 ends.

region.text: Jilin, eastern Liaoning, northern Hebei and the Inner Mongolian steppe edge

ledger.note: 1516: the Ming retreat behind the wall. Cliopatria cuts Jilin, east Liaoning, north Hebei and the steppe edge in 1516; the Great Wall page says 'the outer defenses were gradually moved inward, thereby sacrificing a vital foothold in the steppe transitional zone' without a year. Bridging; the Ordos was 'ruled by descendants of Batumongke Dayan Khan' since 1510 (Ordos Mongols page).
1539: pirates take Shuangyu. The wokou 'started to occupy the island' of Shuangyu (Liuheng Island, off Ningbo); the harbour was razed in June 1548.
1548: Shuangyu destroyed. In June 1548 'Lu Tang then razed the town and rendered the harbour permanently unusable' on Zhu Wan's orders.

region.text: Zhelin, south of Shanghai, and the Huangpu River

ledger.note: 1554: pirate headquarters south of Shanghai. In 1554-1555 the pirates 'placed their headquarters at Zhelin' and in 1555 'Their warships controlled the Huangpu River'; 'Hangzhou, Songjiang, Tongzhou, and Jiaxing were attacked' in 1553-54 and by 1555 '8 out of 11 prefectures of Zhejiang had been ravaged'.

1557: Macau is given to the Portuguese. 'The Portuguese gained consent from the Ming court in 1557 to settle Macau as their permanent trade base in China.' A settlement on sufferance, not a cession of sovereignty; Cliopatria's Ming shape drops Macau only in 1564.

1559: the Yangtze delta is cleared. 'The remaining pirate bands in the Yangtze River Delta were wiped out' in the summer of 1559 (Xu Hai died at Pinghu on 29 September 1556; Wang Zhi was sentenced on 22 January 1560).
1562: Xinghua (Putian) falls to the pirates. 'The prefectural city Xinghua (present-day Putian) was taken after a month-long siege' (December 1562).

region.text: the western Yunnan frontier tusi that Cliopatria's 1564 shape drops

ledger.note: 1563: the Chinese Shan States go to Bayinnaung. 'the Chinese Shan States (1563)' are on the list of the Toungoo conquests; the page names no town. Cliopatria's Ming shape loses 257 cells of western Yunnan in 1564.
1563: the last pirate base in Fujian is destroyed 'by May 1563'.

1567: the Tibetan court relation lapses. Rawski: the Ming's 'unique relationship with Tibetan prelates essentially ended with Jiajing's reign' (1521-1567), and 'the Tibetan lamas discontinued their trips to Ming China and its court'; the Tumed Mongols were moving into Kokonor and the Mongol-Tibetan alliance of 1578 followed.

region.text: western Yunnan and the Kachin-Shan hills of Cliopatria's 1600 shape: page silent; without Kengtung

ledger.note: 1600: the Yunnan frontier is back, bridging. Cliopatria adds 376 cells of Myanmar and 278 of Yunnan to the Ming in 1600; the Taungoo page is silent on Tengyue, Nandian and the Eight Passes, and has 'Ava had seized cis-Salween Shan states by 1604'. Unverified: page budget. Fix fx-09 (F224): Kengtung is left out (Kengtung State page: only a 1405 tusi designation by the Ming).

1618: Nurhaci opens the war in Liaodong. 'The army attacked and captured Fushun, located on the Hun River about 10 kilometers east of Shenyang.' The Ming page: 'In 1618, he openly renounced the Ming overlordship and effectively declared war against the Ming.'
1618: Fushun falls to the Jin. 'The army attacked and captured Fushun'; the Nurhaci page: Li Yongfang 'surrendered Fushun in Liaoning to the Manchus in 1618'.
1618: the Jianzhou Jurchens renounce the Ming. 'In 1618, he openly renounced the Ming overlordship and effectively declared war against the Ming.'
1619: Tieling falls to the Jin. 'Nurhaci continues his campaign subduing Tieling in the summer of 1619'; Kaiyuan is also named as occupied, without its own date.
1621: the Liaodong fighting ends in a Jin victory. 'By May 1621, Nurhaci had conquered the cities of Liaoyang and Shenyang.'

Liaoyang

region.text: the cities of Liaoyang and Shenyang

ledger.note: 1621: Liaoyang and Shenyang fall. 'By May 1621, Nurhaci had conquered the cities of Liaoyang and Shenyang' ('Shenyang fell with the aid of Mongol Ming soldiers in the city'; 'Liaoyang fell after traitors let down ropes', Qing conquest page). Nurhaci made Shenyang his capital in April 1625.

region.text: the Liaodong peninsula and Liaoyang's surroundings: the battle of Guangning, 1622

ledger.note: 1622: the rest of Liaodong goes, bridging. Nurhaci 'killed 16,000 of their soldiers at the battle of Guangning' in 1622; Cliopatria's Ming shape lacks the Liaodong peninsula from 1622, which no page opened explains.
1637: Joseon breaks with the Ming. Defeated in the second Manchu invasion (1636-37), 'King Injo was forced to end his relations with the Ming and recognize the Qing as suzerain instead.'
1642: Jinzhou surrenders. 'The commander of Jinzhou, Zu Dashou, also defected on 8 April 1642, handing them the city.' The Ningyuan-Shanhai corridor stays Ming to 1644.

union.text: Wuchang

region.text: Wuchang, Hunan and part of Jiangxi

ledger.note: 1643: Zhang Xianzhong takes Wuchang and proclaims himself 'Xi Wang' (King of the West). He 'took Macheng in Huguang' and, 'after the capture of Wuchang', 'controlled much of Hunan and part of Jiangxi'. Rebel-held land, hatched.
1643: Li Zicheng holds Xiangyang. 'By 1643, Li had captured Xiangyang.' The page's lead gives 1643; the Cliopatria Li Zicheng shape has northern Hubei from 1642.

1643: Li Zicheng takes Xi'an and Shaanxi. 'After assigned his subordinate to command Tongguan, Li Zicheng proceeded again to Xi'an' in late 1643; the page gives no month for the entry. On the New Year of 1644 he founded the Shun there.
1644: Ryukyu's Ming tribute passes to the Southern Ming. The Ryukyu page: 'Tributary state of the Southern Ming (1644-1646)'; the body text gives no end date for the Ming tribute.
1644: Li Zicheng takes Shanxi. 'In March, his armies had captured the important city of Taiyuan in Shanxi.' The page names the city, the province is the reading.

1644: Beijing falls to Li Zicheng. 'Beijing fell to a rebel army led by Li Zicheng' (24 April on the Qing conquest page, 25 April on the Ming page); 'the emperor hanged himself the next day on a hill behind the Forbidden City'. Wu Sangui opened Shanhai Pass and the Manchus and Wu entered the capital on 6 June.

region.text: the Ming at its end: the north to Li Zicheng's Shun, Liaoxi to the Qing, the south to the Southern Ming

ledger.note: 1644: the Ming end at Beijing. 'On 25 April 1644, Beijing fell to a rebel army led by Li Zicheng' and the Chongzhen Emperor hanged himself; the Hongguang Emperor was crowned at Nanjing 'on June 19' and the Southern Ming carry the south. Li's Shun holds the north-west and Beijing, the Qing take Beijing on 6 June.

wars.name: Ming conquest of Yunnan
wars.outcome: Ming victory: the Yuan prince of Liang died on 6 January 1382 and Dengchuan, the last Dali stronghold, fell in February 1383.
wars.note: The page gives Date '1381-1382' and Result 'Ming victory'; the Ming page says 'In 1381'.

wars.name: Ming-Northern Yuan wars of the Hongwu era

zones.text: Yingchang and the steppe south of the Gobi

wars.outcome: Ming victories at Karakorum (May 1370), Yingchang (June 1370) and Buir Lake (1388); the Yuan court survives as the Northern Yuan on the steppe.
wars.note: 1372: 'Xu Da leading a 150,000-strong army from Shanxi through the Gobi to Karakorum'.

wars.name: Ming campaign against Naghachu
wars.outcome: Naghachu surrendered and the Ming took Manchuria (1387) and the Liaodong peninsula (1388).
wars.note: The Ming page links an article 'Ming military campaign against Naghachu' that was not opened.

wars.name: Ming-Mong Mao War
wars.outcome: Two Möng Mao rebellions (1386-1389, 1397-1398) were put down; no border moved.

wars.name: Yongle Emperor's campaigns against the Mongols
wars.outcome: Inconclusive: 'Weakening of both sides; Status quo ante bellum'; the Emperor died on 12 August 1424 on the return from the fifth campaign.
wars.note: Five expeditions: 25 March 1410 (Onon, 15 June), 6 April 1414, 12 April 1422, 1423 and 1424. The page describes no lasting Ming gain on the steppe.

wars.name: Fourth Chinese domination of Vietnam / Lam Sơn uprising
wars.outcome: The Ming took Đại Ngu in 1406-07 and held it as the province of Jiaozhi (1407-1427); the Lam Sơn rebels, rising on 7 February 1418, won the decisive battle on 7 November 1426 and the Ming withdrew in December 1427.
wars.note: The Lam Sơn uprising page (also opened) gives the stages.

wars.name: Luchuan-Pingmian campaigns
wars.outcome: Ming victory on the infobox, four campaigns (December 1438, 27 February 1441, March 1443, March 1449); Si Renfa executed in January 1446; the last campaign 'ended inconclusively'.

wars.name: Tumu Crisis
wars.outcome: Mongol victory at Tumu (1 September 1449 on the Tumu page, 8 September on the Ming page); Esen reached Beijing on 27 October and withdrew; 'There were no territorial changes'.
wars.note: The Zhengtong Emperor returned in September 1450.

wars.name: Ming-Mongol border wars to the Altan Khan peace
wars.outcome: The 1550 invasion reached the suburbs of Beijing; walls were built at Xuan-Da (1544-49) and Jizhou-Changping (1569-71); 'Altan Khan eventually made peace with China when it opened border cities for trade in 1571'.

wars.name: Jiajing wokou raids
wars.outcome: 'Ming victory': the pirate bases at Shuangyu (1548), the Yangtze delta (1559) and Xinghua (1563) were destroyed and the sea ban was lifted in 1567.
wars.note: Pirates held islands and a few towns, never a province; drawn as small hatched patches.

wars.name: Imjin War (Ming relief of Joseon)
wars.outcome: 'Ming China intervened on the side of the Koreans, sending a large force in 1593'; no Ming border moved.
wars.note: The Imjin War article was not opened; the Joseon page is the source.

wars.name: Ming-Later Jin war
wars.outcome: The Jin took Fushun (1618), Tieling (1619), Shenyang and Liaoyang (1621) and Jinzhou (8 April 1642); the Ming held the Ningyuan corridor until Wu Sangui opened Shanhai Pass in 1644.
wars.note: 'In February 1626, the Jurchens besieged Ningyuan but suffered a defeat in which Nurhaci was mortally wounded.'

wars.name: Late Ming peasant rebellions

zones.text: Shaanxi, Henan, Hubei, Hunan and Shanxi

wars.outcome: Li Zicheng took Xiangyang (1643), Xi'an (late 1643), Taiyuan (March 1644) and Beijing (April 1644); Zhang Xianzhong took Wuchang (1643) and Sichuan (1644). The Ming ended.
wars.note: Li Zicheng rose at Mizhi in 1629; Zhang Xianzhong 'joined the rebel forces in Mizhi County' about 1630.

certainty.note: The Ming's early frontiers are approximate: the steppe edge, Tibet, the south-western tusi and Annam (1407-1427); the provincial borders inside are the Yuan ones.

The northern frontier follows the Great Wall once it is built (the Yulin wall approved on 20 December 1472 and finished in 1474; the Xuan-Da walls completed in 1548; the Jizhou-Changping towers 1569-71) and is firmer there; Tibet, the south-west and the Manchurian side stay soft.

notes:
Written by ea-07 on 2026-10-25 from the 26 pages listed in sources, opened by WebFetch, against a budget of 9: four of the pages opened (Ming dynasty military conquests, Hetao, Ordos Mongols, History of Yunnan) were thin or silent on the Ming borders, so the budget was exceeded to reach the Hongwu, Qing-conquest, Great Wall, Tibet, Hami, Nurgan and Luchuan-Pingmian pages that the shape changes need. Quotes in notes are as WebFetch returned them.

Cliopatria rows to correct. The row begins in 1375 but the Ming began on 23 January 1368: three new keyframes (1368, 1369-70, 1371-73) rebuild the conquest from Zhu's Wu; the 1375 shape holds Liaoning and Jilin 12 years before the Hongwu page dates Manchuria (1387) and Liaodong (1388). The Amur lands (1409-1435) and Hami (1404-1513) are vassal tint, not direct rule; the 1440+ shapes drop Hami 70 years too early. The 1619-1642 shapes drop Liaoning too early (Liaoxi stayed Ming to 1642-44) and the 1632-1641 'Li Zicheng' shapes (and the Ming's loss of Shanxi in 1636) are wrong: Li held no land before 1643 and Shanxi was Ming until March 1644. The 1673-1682 Southern Ming shapes belong to Wu Sangui's Zhou and Taiwan to the Kingdom of Tungning (see southern-ming).

Not settled (page budget or page silent): the Qinghai/Gansu/Ningxia expansion of the 1402 shape and its 1468 withdrawal (no page dates the Western Mongol guards or the Hexi retreat; the ledger carries them at confidence 1); the Inner Mongolia steppe, where Cliopatria keeps two thirds as Ming to 1449 although the Yongle page says no Ming forces stood north of the Great Wall after 1403 except Kaiping (to 1430); the 1516 retrenchment; the western Yunnan frontier (1563-64 loss, 1600 return: the Taungoo page names 'the Chinese Shan States (1563)' and nothing else); the Three Guards/Uriankhai, Dayan Khan and Altan Khan's Tumed in Hetao and Kokonor; Ming-Dai Viet under the Mac (1540); the Bozhou rebellion (1599-1600) and the Dutch at Penghu; the Nine Garrisons list; Joseon was a Ming tributary 1401-1637 on the Joseon page, not 1395-1571 as Cliopatria's allegiance row has it. Tibet as a vassal 1371-1567 is contested (Goldstein: 'no real administrative authority'); drop the tint if the colour agent prefers.

Disagreements between pages: the Tumu battle is 1 September 1449 (Tumu page) or 8 September (Ming page); Beijing fell on 24 April (Qing conquest page) or 25 April 1644 (Ming page, list of emperors); the capital moved in 1421 (Great Wall page), was designated on 28 October 1420 (Ming page infobox) or in 1403 (Ming page text); the Hongwu page puts Liaodong's annexation in 1388 and no page opened mentions an earlier Liaodong command, so Cliopatria's 1375 inclusion of Liaoning is treated as premature (adjust).

Counterparts and states: xi-dynasty, wu-sangui-s-zhou, jianzhou-jurchens and haixi-jurchens are written by ea-07 (see their dossiers). 'Qara Del (Hami)', 'Duan family of Dali', 'Nurgan Jurchens' and 'Wokou pirates' are named, not slugs. The Yuan prince of Liang (Yunnan 1381-82) and Naghachu (Manchuria 1387) are recorded against northern-yuan, which is only the nearest dossier. The qing-dynasty dossier (ea-08) records the Southern Ming and 1673 losses against southern-ming; they should read wu-sangui-s-zhou for 1673-1681.
